title: An Executor Agent cannot finish terminating until its supervision duties are transferred to other Executors
content:
A.1.14.5.2.1 imposes stricter termination duties on Executor Agents than on Primes: the wind-down "must ensure that any affected Prime Agents are able to continue their day-to-day operations without interruptions," any suspension of services "must have a sufficiently elongated period of notice to allow Prime Agents and other stakeholders to obtain alternative support," and — decisively — "An Executor Agent cannot conclude an Agent Termination Protocol until all supervision arrangements are transferred smoothly to other Executor Agents."

The asymmetry is a direct consequence of A.1.14.3.2, which makes an active Executor Accord a condition of a Prime Agent being active at all. An Executor exiting without a successor would not merely inconvenience its counterparties — it would deactivate them. The termination right is therefore conditional on continuity, not on the Executor's own readiness to leave.

This is what makes the mandatory-counterparty requirement tolerable. A dependency you are forbidden to remove is only safe if the party you depend on is forbidden to abandon you, and if replacements are interchangeable — which is precisely the payoff of standardizing Executor Artifacts under A.1.14.2.9.

The broader Prime termination process in A.1.14.5.2 shows the same protective instinct pointed at users: the Executor must ensure cessation of functionality "is clearly communicated and signaled to users or other stakeholders, with a wind-down period calibrated to enable a smooth transition," while the Core Facilitator oversees the wind-down for alignment with "Sky Core and end users' interests" and mediates disputes under A.1.14.5.4. In both cases exit is a supervised process owed to third parties, not a unilateral right.
description: Wind-down must let affected Prime Agents continue uninterrupted, with notice long enough to obtain alternative support — so infrastructure providers cannot exit before successors exist.
